home.title: Talk first. Meet both ways.
home.eyebrow: The dating app where you talk first
home.lead: No swipe, no catalogue, no score. An agent gets to know you in your own words, then opens a small batch of people who fit you in both directions.
home.principlesLead: What Yasakia refuses is as important as what it does.

talk.title: A conversation, not a form
talk.text: The agent asks one question at a time, with humour, in your language.

batch.title: Three to five people, not a feed
batch.text: A small batch, each with why you two in words — never a score.

both.title: Both ways, or not at all
both.text: Someone appears only if you fit them and they fit you.

debrief.title: The next batch waits for you
debrief.text: You debrief the last one first, so every batch fits better than the one before.

home.closingLead: Yasakia is open source, on the same foundations as Orochia and Orazaka. Read the code, or tell us what you expect from a dating app.

works.label: What works today
works.lead: Not released yet, but these parts already run in the code, tested in the code.

location.title: Your location, about 1 km
location.text: A phone's position is rounded to a grid of about 1 km before it is stored. The exact one never reaches the database.

radius.title: Matching inside the radius you choose
radius.text: You set the distance you accept, in kilometres. Matching uses PostgreSQL's earthdistance on the stored position.

signin.title: Sign in by e-mail code or password
signin.text: A 6-digit code arrives by e-mail, or sign in with a password. A forgotten password is reset by code, and every other session ends.

talk.title: An agent you talk to first
talk.text: One question at a time, in your language, in your own words — no form, no swipe. What it understood is shown back to you, the sensitive part sealed.

portrait.title: A portrait in words, never a score
portrait.text: When it knows enough, the agent writes who you are and who you look for, and embeds both. You can read it.

batch.title: Your first batch, three to five people
batch.text: People who fit you and for whom you fit too — the weaker of the two directions decides — each with why you two, in words. Fewer than three: you wait, nobody is made up.

debrief.title: Answering a batch and the debrief
debrief.text: Interested, tell me more or pass — then three quick questions before the next batch.

intros.title: Introductions
intros.text: Seven days to talk when you both said yes. Every message is typed by you two: the agent writes nothing for you and never reads your conversation. Continue together, or let it fade.

how.title: How it works
how.lead: The whole loop, from the first question to the first message — what the app is built to do.

talk.title: 1 · You talk
talk.text: An AI agent gets to know you, one question at a time, in your language.

batch.title: 2 · A small batch opens
batch.text: Three to five people, never a catalogue. Each comes with the reasons you two fit, written in words.

both.title: 3 · It goes both ways
both.text: Filters and fit are checked in both directions: nobody is shown to someone who would not be shown to them.

debrief.title: 4 · You debrief
debrief.text: Tell the agent what you thought of the batch. The next one waits for that debrief, and fits better.

privacy.position: Your position is rounded to about one kilometre before it is stored.
privacy.photos: Photos are re-encoded to strip every metadata block, GPS included, and shown only to someone in your batch or your intro, through a link that expires in minutes.
privacy.realPeople: Real people: 4 to 6 photos, at least 2 showing your face, and a batch opens only once Orazaka — Krizaka’s own AI platform — has checked them: a face is the subject, nothing is written over a photo, no screenshots, nobody who looks under 18. It never identifies anyone. Comparing your photos with each other is biometric processing: it is off until it has been reviewed, and even then only with your separate, explicit agreement, and nothing is kept. It can be wrong; a refused photo is replaced, never punished.
privacy.typed: Every message is typed by a person: the agent writes nothing for you and never reads your conversation. A small mark before each message says whether it looks written by hand, uncertain, probably generated, or too short to judge — a signal, not a verdict, never a number, and it never blocks a message. These detectors are unreliable, especially on short texts and on French or non-native writing: how the message was typed counts as much as its text, and the signal says so.
privacy.media: Photos, videos and voice messages can be sent in a conversation — as they are, nothing is edited — within limits, privately, and only after a safety check; they disappear with the conversation.
privacy.encrypted: Sensitive answers are encrypted at rest.
privacy.control: Export and deletion of your data are in the API from day one; blocks and reports work at once.
privacy.honest: No demo mode and no fake profile: where there is nothing real, nothing is shown.

how.stackLead: One database does the heavy lifting; no broker, no swipe engine.

stack.db: PostgreSQL with pgvector for who you are and who you seek, and the radius.
stack.ui: Krizaka UI, web and native — the same components as the other Krizaka products.
stack.ai: Orazaka for the agent; it never leaves Krizaka's own stack.

demo.title: Demo
demo.lead: Recorded on the development site, against the real engine: a test persona talks to the agent until it writes her portrait, opens her first batch, answers it, sends the debrief, and writes in the introduction that opens. Not an animation, not a mock-up, and not edited: one run, sped up while the agent thinks.
demo.note: Camille is a test persona and the people she meets are a fictional cast: nobody here exists, there is no photo, and Yasakia has no members. The fictional cast says yes back, which is how a yes both ways can be shown; a real person answers in their own batch. The agent’s words are generated live by Orazaka — the model is not scripted — so a run differs from the next. No e-mail is shown: the account’s address is replaced by the persona’s name on screen. Honest note: this recording was made before 2026-10-17 and still shows a first line suggested by the agent — Yasakia no longer offers it, every message is typed by the person; a new recording replaces this one.
demo.nextText: Its own recording, made on the real application, replaces these. Until then: the code is public.
demo.journeyTitle: Talk, a batch, a yes both ways, an introduction
demo.journeyLead: The whole loop, as a person lives it — in one recording.
demo.journeyLabel: Recording: a person talks to the agent, gets her portrait and a batch of five people with the reasons in words, answers each one, sends the debrief, then writes in the introduction that opened.

cues.talk: Camille — a test persona, a fictional adult — opens the talk. She speaks first.
cues.first: She says who she is and where she lives. The agent answers with a question, not a form.
cues.understood: A perfect Saturday, what matters to her. The agent writes down what she said, and nothing more.
cues.portrait: Her portrait is written, in words, from what she said — and embedded, so it can be compared with the others.
cues.look: She asks for her first batch: people who fit her, and for whom she fits too.
cues.shown: Five people, each with why you two — in words, both ways. No score, no swiping. A fictional cast made for tests.
cues.answer: « Tell me more » opens who one of them hopes to meet, in their own words.
cues.yes: She says yes. He said yes too: an introduction opens, for seven days.
cues.answered: She passes on the others. Everyone is answered.
cues.debrief: Three questions before the next batch: did the reasons ring true, what mattered, what next.
cues.intro: The introduction opens. Nobody writes for her: the agent writes no line and never reads what follows.
cues.line: She types her own message. From here, two people talk.
